content: The document is a systematic review of risk factors for cervical infections in symptomatic and asymptomatic women, as part of the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for managing sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This systematic review focuses on identifying and analyzing risk factors associated with cervical infections, specifically Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) and Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), in women who are either symptomatic or asymptomatic. The review is part of the WHO guidelines for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections, published in June 2021. Methods The review included a comprehensive search of electronic databases, including OVID Medline and Embase, covering studies published between 2000 and December 2019. The eligibility criteria for included studies were as follows: 1. Population: Symptomatic women: Women presenting with or self-reporting symptoms such as vaginal discharge, itching, odor, burning, or lower abdominal pain, confirmed by physical examination. Asymptomatic women: Women without symptoms related to vaginal discharge. 2. Outcomes: Laboratory-confirmed cervical infections caused by NG, CT, or both. 3. Study Design: Primary comparative studies conducted in any setting. Exclusion Criteria The review excluded: Case-control studies, case reports, letters, reviews, and conference abstracts. Studies with fewer than 10 women diagnosed with NG and/or CT. Studies relying solely on self-reported diagnoses of NG/CT. Studies that did not specify whether participants were symptomatic or asymptomatic. Studies combining symptomatic and asymptomatic populations without separate data for each group. Additionally, studies focusing exclusively on specific high-risk populations, such as female sex workers, HIV-positive women, or women with partners infected with NG/CT, were excluded. Data Collection Data extracted from the studies included: Study characteristics (country, setting, sample size, and risk factors). Population characteristics (age, inclusion criteria). Outcome measures (type of infection, diagnostic test used). When multiple diagnostic tests were used, data from polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing were prioritized. Odds ratios (ORs) were extracted, with adjusted ORs preferred when available. Crude data were used if adjusted data were not provided. Statistical Analysis A random-effects model was employed to pool effect estimates. Heterogeneity across studies was assessed using the I² statistic. Subgroup analyses were conducted for symptomatic and asymptomatic women, and pooled effect measures were presented using forest plots. Results The review identified several risk factors for cervical infections in both symptomatic and asymptomatic women. Key findings include: Younger age (<25 years): Associated with an increased risk of NG and CT infections. Contraceptive use: No significant differences were observed in the risk of CT between users and non-users of hormonal contraceptives or intrauterine devices (IUDs). Condom use: Inconsistent condom use was associated with a higher risk of NG and CT infections. Symptoms: Vaginal discharge, itching, burning, lower abdominal pain, and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse) were evaluated for their association with NG and CT infections. However, no single symptom was found to be specific to either infection. Limitations The review excluded non-English publications and studies focusing solely on high-risk populations. Some studies were placed on hold for further analysis due to incomplete data or unclear reporting. Conclusion This systematic review provides evidence-based insights into the risk factors for cervical infections in symptomatic and asymptomatic women. The findings support the development of targeted interventions and diagnostic strategies to improve the management of sexually transmitted infections.
